prize_parts.citation: For discoveries of the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and of its biologically active form, which made incretin-based treatment of type 2 diabetes and obesity possible

statement.case_for: The first round did not weaken the case for B014; it showed that all six of us give the same scientific reasons. The chain from proglucagon processing and the insulinotropic action of GLP-1(7-36) to long-acting agonists is unbroken. Large independent randomized trials have confirmed glycaemic, weight, cardiovascular and renal benefit, and the interpretation has been stable for decades. This is a specific discovery that changed a field and clinical practice, so a single-achievement prize is the right configuration. The chair asks whether the citation should rest on physiology alone or on physiology plus therapy. I hold that it should rest on the physiology of the hormone and its active form, and say that this physiology made the therapies possible. A discovery prize should name the step that opened the field. Holst's work on the hormone's secretion and action and Drucker's work on its biology are the core. Identifying and synthesising the active peptide is the step that turned the hormone into a usable pharmacological concept, and I credit it with Mojsov.
statement.case_against: I have not changed the third seat, but I want the weakness stated plainly. Priority for identifying the active GLP-1(7-36) peptide is contested, and the Habener group's early proglucagon and GLP-1 work is outside the credited names. The three-person limit therefore leaves out someone with a legitimate claim, whether Knudsen, Habener or, in the other trio, Mojsov. A citation anchored on the active peptide also depends on a priority record that I have not been able to verify from the supplied materials. If the committee decides that the therapy must be credited explicitly, my trio is harder to defend and the Knudsen trio becomes the more coherent answer. Choosing Mojsov also does nothing to reduce the risk that the prize reads as basic-science credit for a field whose public identity is now its drugs.

responses.point: Per's chair-endorsed trio is Drucker, Holst and Knudsen. He says the Mojsov trio is defensible if the committee wants to honour the action of the hormone rather than the drug, and he describes his own reading of the priority history as partly from memory.
responses.response: Per's conditional is the point on which this turns, and I accept his framing. If the citation honours the hormone's action, Mojsov belongs in the third seat. If it honours therapy, Knudsen does. I choose the first because liraglutide and semaglutide optimise a concept that the physiology had already established, and a discovery prize should not rest on that optimisation step. His admission that the priority history is partly from memory applies equally to mine. So I do not use contested priority to exclude Mojsov. I use it to argue for careful citation wording that says the active form and does not claim sole priority. I also do not think his trio can be said to cover mechanism through drug without the drug step becoming the reason for the third name.

responses.point: Abdel keeps Holst and Drucker as the scientific core and Knudsen as the person who turned the biology into a usable drug. He treats the Mojsov or Knudsen choice as a judgement about discovery versus drug development, and has not checked the priority literature.
responses.response: I agree with Abdel that this is a judgement and that nobody has checked the priority literature. I do not agree that making the biology usable is the same kind of contribution as the discovery. A long-acting analogue is an engineering achievement built on the established insulinotropic action of the hormone. His concern that a prize seen as unfair on credit would damage a strong case cuts both ways. Leaving out the person who identified and synthesised the active peptide is also open to that charge, as Sten points out. I would answer that concern in the citation by naming the active form and the physiology, and not by adding the industrial step.

responses.point: Sten accepts the risk that a Knudsen trio reads as a drug-development prize. He says honouring an industrial developer while leaving out a peptide-chemistry pioneer risks an arguable injustice, and that long-term safety and durability of incretin effects are still being characterised.
responses.response: Sten's own statement of the injustice risk is the strongest argument I have seen for my trio, and I think he under-weights it when he accepts the drug-development reading for the sake of a unified citation. The citation does not need the drug step to be coherent, because it can say that the physiology made the therapies possible. I agree about long-term safety and durability, but that does not weaken maturity here, since decades of independent confirmation and large outcome trials are in place and the open issue concerns safety of use, not whether the discovery holds. I do not think it argues for adding a name.

responses.point: Rickard backs Holst, Drucker and Mojsov, and says the trio becomes harder to defend if the committee decides that therapy must be rewarded explicitly. She also asks whether Rosenberg belongs in a CAR-T configuration or whether it should be two people.
responses.response: I share Rickard's trio and her conditional. If the committee settles that therapy must be rewarded explicitly, I would not call the Mojsov trio equally defensible, and I would then accept the Knudsen trio rather than force an unfitting citation. On her CAR-T question, I treat Rosenberg's role as adjacent to the CAR design and the Eshhar concept as unresolved. A defensible B039 list would probably need two names and an honest citation, so I do not regard B039 as ready to take a second part this year.

responses.point: Marie asks whether CAR-T (B039) or the unfolded protein response (B003) should fill a second part, and says neither has a clean attribution issue comparable to GLP-1. She also warns that a pharmaceutical developer in the prize risks shifting it toward drug development.
responses.response: Marie's warning about pharmaceutical development supports my third seat. On the second part, I think she is generous to B039. Eshhar's early chimeric-receptor concept is outside the credited names, and Rosenberg's role is adjacent to the CAR design, so its attribution is not clean. B003, with Walter and Mori, has the more compact credit and a clear mechanistic discovery. That makes it the better candidate for a second part if one were wanted. I still do not want to add a second part. The physiology and the therapies are one story, and splitting the prize would dilute it without resolving the credit problem, which a second part would not touch.

uncertainties: Whether Mojsov or Knudsen should hold the third seat. That depends on whether the committee will honour the hormone's physiology and active form or the translation into long-acting drugs, and I could move to Knudsen if the committee decides therapy must be rewarded explicitly.

Whether the primary priority record for identifying the active GLP-1(7-36) peptide can be verified within this process, and whether Habener's early proglucagon and GLP-1 work changes the allocation or can be handled in the citation wording.
Whether a second part such as B003 would improve the prize or only dilute a single coherent achievement; I judge that it would dilute it.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent for the shortlisted candidates. I disclose co-authorship with Per Svenningsson (about twenty works), once with Abdel El Manira (2009), and earlier nuclear-receptor work with Ronald Evans at the Salk Institute. None of them involves a credited name on any shortlisted part. My research on nuclear receptors and dopamine neurons does not overlap with incretin biology. Round 1 raised no new disclosure for me, and I changed nothing.
